lesson.title: Unicast, Multicast, Anycast: Who an IPv6 Address Actually Reaches
lesson.summary: IPv6 defines three address types, unicast for one specific interface, multicast for a group of interfaces, and anycast for the nearest of several interfaces sharing an address, and drops IPv4's broadcast entirely in favor of multicast.
lesson.body:
Now that the mechanics of writing and compressing an IPv6 address are established, the next question is what an address actually means once a packet is sent to it: exactly one destination, several destinations, or the nearest of several candidates. IPv6 formally defines three address types to answer that, and it is worth naming upfront what it does not have: unlike IPv4, IPv6 has no broadcast address type at all. Every function that IPv4's broadcast served, such as reaching every host on a local segment at once, is instead handled through specific, well-defined multicast groups, which is both more efficient and more precise.

Unicast is the most familiar type: a unicast address identifies exactly one network interface, and a packet sent to a unicast address is delivered to that single interface only. Within unicast, IPv6 further distinguishes global unicast addresses, which are globally routable on the public internet and typically begin with the 2000 double-colon slash 3 range, covering addresses whose first three bits are 001, from link-local addresses, which are confined to a single physical or logical link and never routed beyond it. Every IPv6-enabled interface automatically gets a link-local address, always drawn from the fe80 double-colon slash 10 block, and uses it for tasks like neighbor discovery and the address autoconfiguration process, regardless of whether it also holds a global address.

Multicast addresses identify a group of interfaces, potentially on different hosts and even different networks, and a packet sent to a multicast address is delivered to every interface that has joined that group. IPv6 multicast addresses are easy to recognize because they always begin with the first eight bits set to 1, written as the prefix ff00 double-colon slash 8. Multicast is how IPv6 replaces IPv4's broadcast: instead of a single all-hosts broadcast address that indiscriminately interrupts every device on a segment, IPv6 defines specific multicast groups for specific purposes, for example ff02 double-colon 1 addresses all nodes on the local link, and ff02 double-colon 2 addresses all routers on the local link, so only devices that actually care about a given message need to process it.

Anycast is the type unique to IPv6's formalized design, though a similar idea existed informally in IPv4 routing. An anycast address is assigned to multiple interfaces, typically on different physical devices, but a packet sent to that address is delivered to only one of them, whichever one is nearest according to the routing protocol's measure of distance. There is no distinct syntax that marks an address as anycast; any unicast address can be provisioned as an anycast address by assigning it to more than one interface, and the network's routing tables handle steering traffic to the closest instance.

This is exactly the technique that lets globally distributed services, like root DNS servers, use one address that resolves to whichever nearby server instance can answer fastest, hiding that geographic distribution from the client entirely, and it is a direct practical payoff of the address format rules covered in the previous section.
